children: The U.K. government cut borrowing in the first six months of its fiscal year, but at a slower pace than planned, underlining the challenges posed by rising prices and higher interest payments as it prepares to deliver its budget next week.

The budget comes as the U.K. is enjoying some time out of the limelight, having been a key focus of concern for investors following surprise tax cuts announced by then Prime Minister Liz Truss in 2022, which led to a sharp fall in the prices of government bonds.

For now, attention has switched to the governments of France and the U.S., both of which have larger budget gaps and debts that are rising much more quickly. Indeed, figures released by the Office for National Statistics on Wednesday suggest the U.K. is on course for a second straight year of declining borrowing.
"The U.K. is one of only a few major economies to be undertaking active fiscal consolidation," economists at BNP Paribas wrote in a note to clients.

That consolidation is not going exactly as planned. The ONS said that government spending exceeded its revenues by 24.5 billion pounds in September, an increase in the budget deficit of 1.8 billion pounds from the same month in 2025.

For the fiscal year to date, borrowing totaled 97.8 billion pounds, a decline of 4.4 billion pounds compared with the same period last year, but 6 billion pounds above projections published by the Office for Budget Responsibility in March.

The overshoot partly reflects the increased costs of providing government services as energy prices have risen since the start of the war between the U.S. and Iran. Higher prices are also raising the cost of paying interest, since the U.K. has a higher share of bonds with payouts linked to inflation than its peers.
The ONS said interest payments were 10.9 billion pounds, an increase of 1.6 billion on the previous year and only the 10th month on record in which monthly payments exceeded 10 billion pounds.

The U.K. government's total debt exceeded 3 trillion pounds for the first time in September. But as a share of GDP, it fell to 94% of gross domestic product from 94.7% a year earlier. New borrowing has also continued to decline as a share of economic output, and was down to 3.1% in the first half of the fiscal year from 3.4% in the same period a year earlier.

According to forecasts released by the International Monetary Fund earlier this month, if the U.K. government were to be able to stick to current plans, its budget deficit would fall to 1.5% of gross domestic product in 2030, well below the 8.4% gap it projects for the U.S., or the 4.2% it forecasts for France. Indeed, it would be the smallest budget gap among members of the Group of Seven advanced economies.

In the same year, the IMF expects the U.K. to have a total government debt roughly equivalent to annual economic output, the second smallest in the G7 after Germany. By comparison, the U.S. is forecast to have a general government debt of 140.7% of GDP.

Economists do not expect to see big changes in tax or spending in the budget. Treasury Chief John Healey was appointed by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham in July, and has a number of reviews of welfare spending to look forward to in 2027, as well as the process of coming up with a multiyear plan for each and every government department.

It may not make sense to make big calls before they are complete, while it is also possible that the war will end soon, paving the way for the stronger economic growth and slower inflation that forecasters expect in the years to the end of the decade.
"Tightening policy now and unwinding this later would then introduce unnecessary volatility in fiscal settings," economists at Investec wrote in a note to clients.

While bond investors may be less concerned about developments in the U.K. than elsewhere, British voters are anxious about the size of the debt, according to a survey of 1,080 adults conducted by Ipsos between Oct. 9 and Oct. 13.

However, voters are divided on how to address the problem, with 35% supporting a reduction in borrowing even if that required less spending, while 28% preferred to increase spending even if it required more borrowing.

"While people are deeply anxious about the state of the public finances and potential market jitters, they remain divided on whether to prioritise debt reduction over public service investment or tax cuts," said Alex Bogdan, a director at polling firm Ipsos.
